item.title: 19 mil reproducciones · 110 reacciones | Eight years ago, photographer Pete McBride almost lost his Colorado home to a wildfire. This summer, he heads back to the flames. Across the American West, an intense fire season is stretching firefighting teams thin. In Colorado, the Gold Mountain Fire has burned over 38,000 acres, while the Aspen Acres Fire has surpassed over 100,000 acres and destroyed hundreds of homes. Decades of drought in the southwest, along with one of the worst snowpacks in recorded history this past winter in the seven-state Colorado River Basin, and record heat waves, have created the perfect conditions for wildfires to escalate. Learn more about what it takes to capture a world on fire: https://on.natgeo.com/MxQCAP | National Geographic

item.title: Six unusual structures identified at Earth's core-mantle boundary with the help of deep learning
item.description: Since scientists can't drill 2,900 km (1,800 miles) to the boundary between Earth's core and deep mantle, they must use information relayed by seismic waves recorded during earthquakes to study this region. In a new study published in the journal JGR Solid Earth, a group of scientists used deep learning to study a large set of a specific type of seismic wave. The analysis revealed six continuous bands of irregularities at the core-mantle boundary (CMB) that had previously appeared only as sparse patches. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Indonesia’s most dangerous fires are burning underground
item.description: Indonesia’s dangerous peat fires are surging early in the 2026 fire season as a strengthening El Niño and severe drought dry out wetlands that can burn underground for months. These slow smoldering fires are especially destructive because they release far more fine particles and several pollutants than typical tropical forest fires, while thick smoke can make them difficult for satellites to detect. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.description: A living shoreline project in New Smyrna Beach largely survived Hurricane Matthew's severe winds. This natural approach used vegetation and sand to stabilize the coast effectively. item.title: Typhoon Saudel: days of flooding trigger fatal landslide in central China
item.description: At least one person was killed and 11 are missing after they were buried by a landslide in central China as the region continued to battle severe flooding caused by Typhoon Saudel. The landslide hit Gaoping, a town in a mountainous area of Jiangxi province, at around 4am on Saturday, according to state broadcaster CCTV. It said rescue teams were rushing to the disaster site. The accident followed days of torrential rain brought by the outer bands of Typhoon Saudel and a cold front. Floodwaters... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Country diary: The wild, riotous sounds of otters in battle | Cal Flyn
item.description: Isle of Lismore, Argyll: They skim over the surface like stones, making such a hullabaloo you could hear them a mile away I hear them before I see them: a wailing, or something more like ululation. High-pitched, repeated vocalisations that are neither man nor cat, but somewhere in between. I throw open the cabin door, unsure what to look for, and for a moment see nothing new: only the rocky strand and the sweep of dark wrack high above the shoreline. The strange, warbling sound comes again. Ai-ai-ai-ai. Not quite screaming, not quite howling, not quite trilling, but all of those things at… Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.title: Trump order directs officials to consider stripping protections for gray wolves
item.description: Interior department given three months to decide whether wolves can be removed from endangered species list Donald Trump signed an executive order on Friday directing the interior department to consider de-listing gray wolves from the Endangered Species Act and to contemplate whether the agency could make it easier to authorize killing them. item.title: ONU alerta sobre potencia que tendrá fenómeno de El Niño en el mundo
item.description: La ONU alertó que el fenómeno de El Niño será de una categoría muy fuerte y existe la posibilidad de que incluso sea un evento de categoría excepcionalmente fuerte, superando las escalas de medición usadas en las últimas cuatro décadas. El fenómeno natural puede generar tifones, inundaciones y sequías severas en varias partes del mundo, que, según los científicos, cada vez son más potentes por el impacto del cambio climático.
